summary: Makes the US Secure Hash Algorithm 1 conveniently available to the Internet community, with a description and sample code.

plainLanguage.summary: It describes a recipe that turns any message into a short fingerprint.

subtitle: The SHA-1 hash algorithm written out for the Internet community, with reference C code.

tldr.problem: The US government adopted SHA-1 in FIPS 180-1, but the Internet community lacked a convenient, openly available description and code for it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo restates the algorithm: pad the message to a multiple of 512 bits, process it in 512-bit blocks through 80 steps each, and output a 160-bit message digest. It adds a demonstration C implementation.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that makes no independent security claim, and it has been updated by RFC 4634 and RFC 6234.

today: RFC 3174 is an Informational memo that makes SHA-1 conveniently available and makes no independent security claim. It has been updated by RFC 4634 and RFC 6234, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What SHA-1 Does
sections.content:
This document specifies the Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA-1) for computing a condensed representation of a message or data file. When a message of any length less than 2^64 bits is input, it produces a 160-bit output called a message digest. The digest can be fed to a signature algorithm, and signing the digest rather than the whole message often improves efficiency because the digest is much smaller. The verifier of a digital signature must use the same hash algorithm as its creator.

The algorithm is called secure because it is computationally infeasible to find a message that corresponds to a given digest, or to find two different messages that produce the same digest. Any change to a message in transit will, with very high probability, result in a different digest and the signature will fail to verify. Most of the text was taken by the authors from FIPS 180-1, and the assertions of security are made by the US Government, not by the authors; only the C code is original.
sections.plainLanguage: SHA-1 squeezes a message of any size into a small fingerprint. If even one letter changes, the fingerprint almost surely looks completely different.

sections.title: Words, Blocks and Operations
sections.content:
SHA-1 works on 32-bit words, each written as a sequence of 8 hexadecimal digits, and on blocks of 512 bits, which are 16 words. An integer between 0 and 2^32 - 1 can be represented as a word, and an integer z with 0 <= z < 2^64 can be represented as a pair of words.

The algorithm applies the bitwise operations AND, OR, XOR and NOT to words, adds words modulo 2^32, and uses the circular left shift written S^n(X), where X is a word and n is an integer with 0 <= n < 32. The circular shift is defined as the left shift of X by n positions combined with the right shift of X by 32 minus n positions, which is equivalent to rotating X left by n positions.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of Lego bricks of one fixed size. SHA-1 snaps them together and spins them around in set ways.

sections.title: Message Padding
sections.content:
SHA-1 processes 512-bit blocks in sequence, so the message is first padded to make its total length a multiple of 512. On the right of the message, a single 1 bit is appended, then enough 0 bits so that the last 64 bits of the last block are free, and then the length of the original message in bits is written as a 64-bit integer, the two-word representation of the length.

The worked example pads the five-byte message abcde, which is 40 bits. After the 1 bit there are 407 zero bits, making 448 bits, and the final two words are the hexadecimal value for 40. The padded message is then regarded as a sequence of blocks, each of 16 words, and processed one block at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: Before packing a box, you fill the empty space with standard filler and write the item count on the lid, so every box is the same size.

sections.title: Functions, Constants and the Digest
sections.content:
Eighty logical functions f(0) through f(79) and eighty constant words K(0) through K(79) are used, split into four groups of 20 steps. Each function operates on three 32-bit words and produces a 32-bit word, and the constants in hex are 5A827999, 6ED9EBA1, 8F1BBCDC and CA62C1D6 for the four groups of 20.

Five word registers H0 to H4 start with fixed values. Each 512-bit block is divided into 16 words and expanded into an 80-word sequence, then run through 80 steps that update the working words A to E; after each block those working words are added into the registers. After the last block, the message digest is the 160-bit string formed by the five registers. A second method uses a 16-word circular queue instead of an 80-word array; it saves sixty-four 32-bit words of storage but is likely to run slower, and it gives the same digest.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a big mixing machine. Every chunk of the message gets stirred into five numbers, and the final five numbers are the fingerprint.

sections.title: The C Reference Code
sections.content:
Section 7 gives a demonstration C implementation in three parts: a header file, the code file and a test driver. The application programming interface is three calls that reset the context, feed in input and return the result, and the hash size constant is 20 bytes, matching the 160-bit digest.

The code works only on messages whose length is a multiple of 8 bits, and it needs 32-bit and 8-bit unsigned integer types. Its style follows the earlier MD4 and MD5 RFCs, and it clears the internal message block buffer before returning the digest because the message may be sensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Along with the recipe, the authors include a ready-made kitchen tool, written in the C programming language, that follows the recipe exactly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document is intended to give the Internet community convenient open source access to the United States Federal Information Processing Standard secure hash function SHA-1. It states that no independent assertion of the security of this hash function, by the authors, for any particular use is intended. The security statements in the body of the document are made by the author of FIPS 180-1, the US Government.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors copied the recipe but do not promise how strong the lock it makes is. That promise belongs to the people who invented it.
